title: How to Mark and Give Feedback
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles, an English teacher and author, argues that feedback is only worth the name if it makes a student improve, and that roughly a third of the feedback teachers give actually makes students worse. Drawing on cognitive load, he says to give only the one to three pieces of feedback students will actually practise, and to give none without a plan for acting on it. His central device is making abstract advice concrete: use the visualiser to show errors and corrections live, and teach from model answers that display three or four excellent features. He insists students should redo the same exam question after feedback, since that is the only precise test of whether the feedback was understood. A worked Dickens-to-Harry Potter soundscape example shows how one model differentiates itself to each student. The post closes with a list of further techniques from his book.
points: Feedback counts only if it improves the student; roughly a third of it backfires, so receptiveness and working-memory limits should govern how much is given.
Limit feedback to one point, or three or four at most, and give none unless students have a planned opportunity to act on it.
Advice such as use embedded quotations is abstract to many students; putting their work under a visualiser and correcting it live makes it concrete.
Having students redo the same question after feedback isolates whether they understood the feedback, whereas moving to a new text confounds it.
A single strong model, such as Dickens adapted to Harry Potter, differentiates automatically because students imitate only what they can currently understand.
quotes: Feedback is only what makes a student improve. Anything intended as feedback which doesn’t then make the student improve is just noise.
Approximately a third of the feedback we offer actually makes students worse. Students need to be receptive to the feedback they receive.

Only give feedback to students on what you want them to practise. Your skill is to weigh up the 10 pieces of advice or success criteria you could give them, and pick the one which will have most impact.

But, morally speaking, if you don’t have a plan for making the students act on those points of feedback, don’t give them. Otherwise your feedback and action points will become pointless and demotivating for students, and a waste of your time.

However, the moment we put the student’s work under the visualiser and show where the error is, and then talk through and write the correction, the abstract becomes concrete. Students can now literally see what you mean.
Not really. Remember, we assume our feedback on the student’s answer has been concrete. But how do we know? There is only one way. Ask the student to write their answer to the same question again.
I know that the model will differentiate to each student. They will automatically pick some of Dickens’ other skills in their own version, and this will be completely concrete to them.
